Indu: he said “is your brain on holiday” in front of everyone
Ishita: I know, I was there. I'm sorry. The whole room went so quiet
Indu: I wanted to disappear
Ishita: what happened after class?
Indu: Sir, our maths teacher, asked me to stay back. He said he'd spoken sharply, it wasn't fair, and my second step was right
Ishita: really??
Indu: and he said he'd say something to the class tomorrow too
(Next day)
Indu: he did. He said “Yesterday I mocked an answer. That's not how we work in this room. We ask, we fix, we don't label.” He didn't say my name
Ishita: the back row stopped smirking
Indu: it still stings a bit. but better

qa.q: What did the teacher say in front of everyone that Indu quotes at the start?
qa.a: He said, “is your brain on holiday” in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Indu feel during the incident, and what shows it?
qa.a: Indu wanted to disappear, which shows in “I wanted to disappear,” and still felt a sting the next day, though a bit better.

qa.q: Why did it help that the teacher spoke privately first and then spoke to the class without naming Indu?
qa.a: The private words repaired the hurt to Indu, and the class talk set a norm without shaming anyone, so neither Indu nor the class was made a target.

qa.q: How might Ishita have seen the class talk the next day?
qa.a: Ishita seems to have felt relief, since Ishita noticed that the back row stopped smirking after the teacher spoke.

grounding: After a humiliating moment, a teacher speaks privately with the student and then addresses the class norm without shaming anyone.

passage: In the small-town school's lab, Tushar's elbow knocked a glass beaker off the bench. It shattered. “Are you stupid?” the science teacher snapped, and half the class laughed. Tushar's ears burned. Ishita, at the next bench, stopped writing. The next morning the teacher called Tushar to the veranda before assembly. “I spoke to you in a way I shouldn't have,” the teacher said. “A beaker costs little. I'm sorry.” Tushar nodded, unsure what to say. Later, in class, the teacher told everyone, “Yesterday some of us laughed at a mistake. In this lab we clear up together, and nobody is laughed at.” Ishita went to fetch the dustpan, and three others followed.

qa.q: Where did the teacher take Tushar the next morning?
qa.a: The teacher called Tushar to the veranda before assembly.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling when Tushar nodded, unsure what to say?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt a mix of relief and awkwardness after the humiliation, and did not know how to answer an adult's apology.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to repair the moment?
qa.a: The teacher apologised privately for the tone, then told the class that nobody is laughed at in the lab and that clearing up is done together, without naming or shaming anyone.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have gone to fetch the dustpan first?
qa.a: Ishita had stopped writing when the beaker broke and seems to have wanted to show that helping, not laughing, is the norm, and three others followed.

grounding: After a humiliating moment, a teacher speaks privately to the student and then sets a class norm without shaming anyone.

passage: In Ms Aiko Mori's Grade 10 English class in Toronto, Rania read her poem aloud and pronounced the s in 'island'. Someone laughed, then half the room joined in, and Rania sat down with her face hot. Ms Mori didn't shout. At lunch she found Rania in the library. 'That laughter was wrong, and I should have stopped it sooner. How are you doing?' Rania shrugged, eyes wet. 'I just want to disappear.' 'Your poem was one of the strongest. Would you like to read it again sometime, or shall I?' The next morning Ms Mori began class without naming anyone. 'Yesterday we laughed at a mistake. In this room, we don't. English spelling is strange; ask me about "colonel" sometime.' A few students laughed, with her this time. Then Liam turned around. 'Your poem was good, Rania.'

qa.q: Which word did Rania mispronounce?
qa.a: 'Island'; she pronounced the s.

qa.q: What did Rania mean by 'I just want to disappear'?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and ashamed after the class laughed, and wanted to hide from everyone.

qa.q: Which of Ms Mori's steps helped repair things, and why?
qa.a: Speaking privately first and owning that she should have stopped it sooner, then naming the class norm the next day without naming anyone.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when turning around to Rania?
qa.a: Liam likely felt a bit guilty about the laughter and wanted to make amends, encouraged by the teacher's reset.

grounding: After a student is laughed at, a teacher speaks with her privately and resets the class norm without shaming anyone.

passage: At the district hockey academy, Damini missed an open goal in the practice match, and the coach shouted across the field, 'Did you leave your brain at home?' Some girls laughed. Yamini didn't. Damini finished practice without a word and skipped the team snack. The next morning, the coach called Damini aside by the equipment shed. 'What I said yesterday was out of line. You were brave to go for that shot. I'm sorry.' Damini nodded, not quite looking up. At the team huddle, the coach said, 'Yesterday I spoke badly to a player. Nobody here gets mocked for a miss, including by me. Misses are how shooters learn.' Yamini squeezed Damini's shoulder. That afternoon, Damini took the penalty stroke in the drill and scored.

qa.q: What did the coach shout when Damini missed?
qa.a: 'Did you leave your brain at home?'

qa.q: What does Damini skipping the team snack suggest?
qa.a: Damini felt humiliated and hurt after the shout and the laughter, and wanted to stay away from the team.

qa.q: What made the coach's repair work?
qa.a: The coach apologised to Damini privately, then set the team rule, including for the coach, without naming Damini.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini, who didn't laugh?
qa.a: Yamini likely felt uncomfortable during the laughter and relieved at the apology, and shows support by squeezing Damini's shoulder.

grounding: A coach repairs a humiliating moment by apologising privately and resetting the team norm without shaming anyone.

passage:
Dear Rehana,
I'm writing because I didn't handle Friday well. When your phone rang during the test and I said, in front of everyone, 'Some people clearly don't care about their future,' I shamed you. I'm sorry. I found out afterwards that it was your mother calling from the hospital.
Today I spoke to the class. I didn't mention you. I said that our rule about phones stays, but that none of us, me included, gets to embarrass anyone in front of others. We agreed that anyone expecting an urgent call can tell me before a test.
If you'd like to talk, I'm in the staffroom after sixth period. You're welcome to bring a friend.
Yogesh Kulkarni
Physics

qa.q: Who was calling when Rehana's phone rang?
qa.a: Rehana's mother, calling from the hospital.

qa.q: What might Rehana have felt after Friday's comment?
qa.a: Rehana likely felt humiliated and hurt, shamed in front of the class while already worried about the call from the hospital.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do to repair things?
qa.a: Apologised privately in writing, then spoke to the class about not embarrassing anyone without naming Rehana, and set a fair rule for urgent calls.

qa.q: How might the rest of the class see the new urgent-call agreement?
qa.a: They may feel it is fairer and safer, knowing even the teacher won't embarrass them and they can explain in advance.

grounding: A teacher repairs a moment of public shaming with a private apology and a class-wide norm that names no one.

passage: Didi, you remember the poem thing? Let me, Hansa, tell it properly this time. I read my monsoon poem in Kamal Sir's class, and from the back someone shouted, "Copied from the internet!" Everybody laughed. Sir laughed a little too, then just said, "Next." I wanted to sink into the floor. The next morning he called me into the corridor before assembly. He said, "Hansa, yesterday I let that go on, and I shouldn't have. I'm sorry. Your poem was yours." Then in class he didn't name anyone. He said, "Yesterday this room got something wrong, including me. If you doubt someone's work, come to me quietly. We don't laugh people out of speaking here." The back row went red and stared at their desks. And didi, last Friday I read again. Nobody laughed except at the funny line.

qa.q: What did someone shout when Hansa read the monsoon poem?
qa.a: Someone shouted, "Copied from the internet!"

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling right after the class laughed?
qa.a: Hansa felt humiliated and wanted to sink into the floor, made worse because Sir laughed a little too.

qa.q: Which of Kamal Sir's steps repaired things, and why?
qa.a: He apologised privately to Hansa first, then set the class norm without naming anyone, so nobody was shamed and trust came back.

qa.q: What might the back row have felt when Sir spoke to the class?
qa.a: They probably felt embarrassed and caught out, but not publicly shamed, which left them room to change.

grounding: Shows a teacher repairing a humiliating moment by speaking privately with Hansa and addressing the class norm without shaming anyone.
